BOC-3 Registration Requirements and Filing Process - LegalClarity

 BOC-3 Registration Requirements and Filing Process 

 A BOC-3 is a federal form that names a person in each required state who can accept legal papers on your behalf as a motor carrier, broker, or freight forwarder. The FMCSA requires every company with interstate operating authority to have this filing before that authority becomes active. Without it, your MC or FF number stays dormant and you cannot legally haul freight, broker loads, or forward shipments across state lines. The filing itself costs nothing to submit to the government, though youll pay a process agent or blanket company to handle it.

 Three types of businesses must file a BOC-3: motor carriers (hauling property or passengers for hire), property brokers , and freight forwarders . The requirement comes from 49 U.S.C. § 13303, which directs every carrier, broker, or freight forwarder operating under federal jurisdiction to designate a written agent for receiving legal notices. 1  Office of the Law Revision Counsel. 49 USC 13303 Service of Notice in Proceedings The regulation implementing that statute, 49 CFR Part 366, spells out the details of who qualifies, which states you need coverage in, and how the form works. 2  eCFR. 49 CFR 366.2 Form of Designation

Once the FMCSA fully implements all Unified Registration System provisions, every motor carrier, including private carriers , will need to file as well. 3  Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration. Designation of Agents for Service of Process If you operate exclusively within one state and hold no federal authority, the BOC-3 requirement does not apply to you.

ceramic.title: FMCSA’s Identity Checks Reshape Registration — But Not How We First Thought
ceramic.snippet: With FMCSA effectively slamming the door on the easiest path for fraudsters (creating fresh carrier identities out of whole cloth), bad actors are likely to pivot their strategies. If you’re a scammer who until now could register a bogus trucking company online and obtain an MC number with stolen or fake credentials, the new facial ID requirement is a serious obstacle. We expect to see increased attempts at hijacking or recycling dormant carrier accounts instead. In fact, industry reports suggest there’s already a black market for existing carrier authorities: organized fraud rings have been buying up old MC numbers in bulk (  overdriveonline.com  ). By purchasing or taking over a defunct or inactive carrier’s identity, criminals can use a “seasoned” authority that looks legitimate, thus bypassing scrutiny on new applications. Some nefarious actors will pay tens of thousands of dollars for a clean, aged MC number with a good safety record, effectively treating it as a commodity to commit freight fraud. Others may resort to outright identity theft – for example, using phishing and social engineering to obtain a carrier’s login credentials or DOT PIN, then changing the company’s contact information to seize control of the account (a practice FMCSA has been fighting since 2023). FMCSA is not oblivious to this shift. The agency’s long-term fraud strategy includes forcing verification on existing accounts as well: eventually every carrier will need to validate their identity when updating registration (  fmcsa.dot.gov  ). This will help root out scammers who managed to infiltrate the system in the past. FMCSA also cracked down on address fraud (requiring a verifiable physical business address) to prevent fake office locations that criminals often used (  freightwaves.com   )  .

ATA challenged several of the agreements requirements, arguing, inter alia, that they are preempted by federal transportation law.  Subject to an express exception for safety regulation, the FAAAA generally preempts any state law, regulation, or other provision having the force and effect of law related to a price, route, or service of any motor carrier . . . with respect to the transportation of property.  A related transportation statute preempts state identification requirements for commercial motor vehicles; it too applies only to state provisions with the force and effect of law.  After a bench trial, the district court found none of the challenged requirements preempted.  A divided panel of the Ninth Circuit affirmed in large part, reversing only as to one requirement that is no longer at issue.

  The Court also granted cert. on a second question: the effect of its 1954 decision,  Castle v. Hayes Freight Lines, Inc  . , on the Ports ability to deny access to carriers for violations of any concession agreement requirements that are not preempted.  (This potentially includes provisions beyond those at issue in the first question presented.)  In  Castle , the Court struck down a state law that punished carriers for repeatedly violating state trucking weight limitations by prohibiting their use of state highways for up to a year.  While noting that states retain authority to impose conventional forms of punishment, the Court explained that the Illinois prohibition was the equivalent of a partial suspension of the carriers federally granted certificate to operate in interstate commerce.  State highways, the Court reasoned, are used to transport interstate goods and serve as connecting links to other states.  Because only the federal government (via the now-abolished Interstate Commerce Commission) had authority to grant certificates to operate, the state prohibition was preempted.

ceramic.title: What Strategic Carriers Evaluate for Filing for a New MC Number
ceramic.snippet:
Advanced Considerations Before Filing for a New MC Number 

 For seasoned carriers, filing for a new Motor Carrier (MC) Number is far more than a procedural step. It is a deliberate act of organizational structuring with regulatory, financial, and operational implications. Each new authority establishes a separate legal and compliance identity that influences how the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), insurers, brokers, and business partners assess the carrier’s credibility.

 An MC Number represents a federal authorization tied to a defined legal entity, carrying its own compliance record, insurance requirements, and operational footprint. Before initiating a new filing, carriers evaluate whether creating a separate authority is strategically justified.

   Potential interactions with existing authorities to avoid redundant reporting or regulatory scrutiny.The FMCSA’s oversight mechanisms now analyze entity linkages across multiple filings, making structural clarity essential for both compliance and operational efficiency.

 The FMCSA scrutinizes filings to identify carriers that attempt to circumvent enforcement through repetitive registrations. Entities with overlapping ownership or shared management across multiple authorities may be flagged for additional review.

 Beyond statutory requirements, the insurance posture of a new MC Number significantly impacts both compliance perception and operational risk. Establishing a new authority effectively resets the carrier’s underwriting history.

 Every new MC Number enters the FMCSA’s New Entrant Safety Assurance Program for an approximately 18-month monitoring period.

  Carriers with mature compliance programs verify that all identifiers — legal names, addresses, EINs, and process agent information — are synchronized prior to filing. Consistency across these data points is critical to establishing a defensible compliance footprint.

jina.title: What Does Inactive Authority Mean for a Carrier?
jina.snippet:
In the commercial trucking world, your **operating authority**is your ticket to do business. It is the official stamp of approval from the [FMCSA](https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/) that allows you to transport goods across state lines for money.

But what happens when you check the [FMCSA SAFER system](https://safer.fmcsa.dot.gov/)and see the word **"Inactive"** next to your name?

An inactive status is an immediate red flag that halts your operations. Let’s look at exactly what this status means, why it happens, and how you can get your trucks back on the road safely.

**🛑 The Core Meaning: You Cannot Operate**

When a carrier's authority is **Inactive**, it means they are **legally forbidden from hauling regulated freight**.

*   **It is illegal:**Moving goods with an inactive status can result in massive federal fines.

*   **Brokers will blacklist you:**Modern freight brokers use automated compliance software. If your authority drops to inactive, you will fail onboarding instantly.

*   **Insurance risks:**Driving with an inactive authority can void your insurance coverage if you get into an accident.

**🔍 Why Does an Authority Become Inactive?**

An operating authority rarely goes inactive by mistake. It usually happens for one of four major compliance or business reasons:

**1. Missed Biennial Updates (Form MCS-150)**

Every two years, the FMCSA requires carriers to fill out **Form MCS-150**. This form updates your fleet size, mileage, and contact info. If you miss your deadline, the FMCSA will deactivate your USDOT number. This automatically turns your operating authority inactive.

To keep your MC number active, your insurance company must file proof of liability coverage directly with the FMCSA. If you cancel your policy, switch providers without updating files, or let your insurance lapse, your authority is quickly pulled.

## An inactive USDOT number concerns the registration  
NOT AUTHORIZED describes authority attached to an active registration. An inactive USDOT number describes the registration itself. Neither label says whether the entity once held authority, why it ended or whether a reinstatement is in progress.  
SAFER’s help text cites 49 CFR 390.19(b)(4) for the inactive value. In the current eCFR, section 390.19 is limited to certain Mexico-domiciled carriers, and the general requirement appears in 49 CFR 390.19T: an update every 24 months on a schedule set by the last two digits of the USDOT number, with penalties and deactivation of the USDOT number for a person that misses it.

Authority Reinstatement

By the Fast Reinstatement compliance team · Reviewed by Korey Sharp-Paar, Founder

DOT reinstatement is the FMCSA process that restores a revoked or suspended USDOT/MC operating authority to ACTIVE on SAFER. webiq.title: Authority Reinstatement Process: When Your MC Goes Inactive
webiq.snippet:
Reinstatement depends on the cause. For an insurance lapse, get a new BMC-91 on file (49 CFR §387.7) and pay FMCSA’s $80 reinstatement fee. A USDOT number deactivated for a missed MCS-150 is reactivated by filing the update (49 CFR §390.19T). A Conditional or Unsatisfactory rating needs a Corrective Action Plan and an upgrade request (49 CFR §385.17). ... FMCSA can revoke a carrier’s operating authority for a handful of reasons: an insurance lapse, a cancelled BOC-3, or a Conditional / Unsatisfactory safety rating from a compliance review. A missed MCS-150 biennial update is different: it deactivates the USDOT number, not the authority. The path back depends on the cause. For an insurance reinstatement, the request is prepared for submission by you or a filer you authorize for $300, FMCSA fee included, once the new BMC-91 is on file; a safety-rating reinstatement requires a Corrective Action Plan. Operating while deactivated can draw civil penalties under 49 USC §14901. ... ** When a BMC-91 expires or cancels and is not replaced within the 30-day cancellation-notice window of 49 CFR §387.313 (d) (Form BMC-35), FMCSA revokes the authority.
**Missed MCS-150 biennial update.** A missed biennial update can lead to civil penalties and deactivation of the USDOT number (49 CFR §390.19T (b) (4)). This deactivates the USDOT number, not the authority, and filing the update reactivates it. See our MCS-150 late filing guide.
**BOC-3 cancellation.** If your blanket process agent cancels the designation, FMCSA no longer has a BOC-3 on file and the authority becomes inactive.
Unsatisfactory ratings impose a 60-day cease-operation order under 49 CFR §385.13. ... Inactive authority with no insurance on file means a new BMC-91. A deactivated USDOT number with the BOC-3 still on file points to a missed MCS-150. Inactive authority with insurance and BOC-3 both on file points to a safety-rating issue. ... Switching insurers is fine; the gap between policies is what leads to revocation.

webiq.title: BOC-3 Filing: What It Is, Who Needs It, and How to File (2026) | Indemni
webiq.snippet:
BOC-3 is a required FMCSA filing that designates process agents for brokers and carriers. Learn what it is, who needs it, and how to file before your authority goes inactive. ... A BOC-3 is the FMCSA “Designation of Agents for Service of Process” meaning a carrier, broker, or freight forwarder names a process agent (or blanket agent network) who can receive court papers and legal notices on their behalf in the states they operate or do business in, and FMCSA expects it on file to obtain and keep active registration.

If you are a motor carrier, broker, or freight forwarder subject to FMCSA registration, you generally need a BOC-3 on file as part of registration, and failing to file can lead to deactivation of the USDOT number under the FMCSA process-agent rules, because the designation is treated as a required condition of active registration. ... FMCSA’s policy statement on invalid BOC-3 filings is blunt: entities must maintain an accurate designation on file to keep registration active, and FMCSA interprets the rules to require a valid designation “at all times” for operating authority registration to remain active. ... In 2026, BOC-3 filing is still handled through FMCSA’s systems and typically submitted electronically by a registered process agent (especially for motor carriers), and you should plan for it as a gating item for authority activation since FMCSA’s registration guidance ties operating authority to having BOC-3 and insurance filings in place, with FMCSA also shifting filers toward portal and Login.gov workflows.  ... FMCSA tells the public to use the Licensing & Insurance (L&I) system to look up a motor carrier, broker, or freight forwarder’s operating authority.  ... webiq.title: Authority Reinstatement Process: 2026 Walkthrough After Revocation or Inactivation
webiq.snippet:
FMCSA authority lapses for a few common reasons: (1) BMC-91 insurance lapse - registration stays in effect only while the carrier keeps its required insurance on file (49 USC §13906 (a) (1)); (2) BOC-3 process-agent designation lapse; (3) a final Unsatisfactory safety rating, which leads to revocation (49 CFR §385.13 (e)); (4) broker authority suspended when the BMC-84 bond or BMC-85 trust falls below $75,000 (49 CFR §387.307 (e)); (5) voluntary revocation. A missed MCS-150 biennial update is different: it can lead to deactivation of the USDOT number (49 CFR 390.19T (b) (4)), and FMCSA's guidance is to file the missing update to reactivate it. ... The carrier must request a rating change in writing with evidence of corrective action (49 CFR §385.17); FMCSA reviews the request within 30 days for passenger and placardable hazmat carriers and 45 days for others, and the rating must be upgraded before operations resume.

A motor carrier with NOT AUTHORIZED status cannot legally operate. Operating as a for-hire property carrier without the required registration exposes the carrier to civil penalties under 49 USC §14901 - a minimum of $13,676 per violation under the current inflation-adjusted schedule in 49 CFR part 386, Appendix B.

you.title: U.S. Air Carriers | US Department of Transportation
you.snippet:
Anyone who wants to provide air transportation service as an air carrier must first obtain two separate authorizations from the Department of Transportation:Economic Authority from the Office of the Secretary of Transportation (the Department) in the form of a certificate for interstate or foreign passenger and/or cargo authoritySafety Authority in the form of an Air Carrier Certificate and Operations Specifications from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)Economic authority for U.S. carriers may be in the form of a certificate for interstate or foreign passengers and/or cargo and mail authority, a certificate for interstate or foreign all-cargo authority, or authorization as a commuter air carrier.
To receive authority from the Department, the air carrier must file an application in the public docket via www.regulations.gov . Separate applications are required to obtain interstate authority and foreign authority.
On the other hand, if an air carrier starts its air service within one year and subsequently ceases that service, its economic authority is automatically suspended and it has one year from the date of the cessation to resume service or that authority will be terminated for dormancy (see section 204.7(b)). Any air carrier proposing to resume service within the one-year period must file with the Department’s Dockets Section, at least 45 days before the date on which service is expected to resume, a notice of such intent and updated fitness information as required by section 204.3.
The air carrier may not recommence service unless and until it is authorized to do so by the Department. If the air carrier wishes to resume air service in less than 45 days, it may request a waiver from the 45-day advance notice requirements of section 204.7. Any such waiver request must be filed with Dockets or uploaded via www.regulations.gov.  A $280 filing fee must be paid on www.pay.gov.

you.snippet:
The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) sets specific insurance requirements in accordance with 49 CFR Part 387 for entities who apply and obtain operating authority registration in accordance with 49 U.S.C. §§ 13906, 31138, and 31139. FMCSA will not grant operating authority registration until the registrant has in effect the minimum levels of financial responsibility on file with FMCSA.
Insurance requirements vary depending on the entity type (motor carrier, broker, freight forwarder) and the entity’s type of operating authority(s), type of cargo, and vehicle type(s). Once operating authority is granted, entities are required to maintain proof of insurance and designation of agents for process on file with FMCSA to avoid revocation proceedings.
Important: FMCSA Portal Account Approval Process for Main Filers and Sub-Filers · To register as an insurance company or financial institution to make financial responsibility filings with the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), filers must comply with applicable requirements under 49 CFR Part 387.

New entities registering with the Agency for the first time should be prepared to contact their financial responsibility provider to request filing of the required forms immediately after obtaining their designated docket number. Once an entity applies for Operating Authority (MC/FF/MX), a financial responsibility provider must file the appropriate insurance form(s) on behalf of the applicant.
